title: Small Bets, Long Games: A Saner Way to Invest in Businesses
excerpt: You don't need a fund to invest in businesses — you need position sizing, patience, and a definition of 'return' that includes what you learn. Our approach to backing companies without betting the house.
content:
Somewhere along the way, "investing in businesses" started to mean either buying index funds or writing six-figure angel cheques. There's a wide, productive middle — putting modest, deliberate capital into real companies — and it's how most durable wealth in most of the world actually gets built. Here's the operating system we use at Alttene, useful whether your unit is thousands or millions.

Size bets so a zero doesn't end you

Private businesses fail often — that's not cynicism, it's the base rate. So the first rule is arithmetic: no single bet should be big enough that losing it changes your life, and the portfolio should be small enough that each bet still gets your attention. For most people that means a handful of positions built slowly over years, not a spray of twenty in a hot quarter.

Invest where you have an unfair information edge

The market rewards you for knowing something true that others don't. You're most likely to hold that edge close to home: the industry you work in, the supply chain you've lived, the community you belong to. The barbershop chain whose unit economics you can see with your own eyes may be a better bet for you than a fintech you read about in a newsletter.

Underwrite the operator, then the terms

In small private deals, the operator is the business. Before any money moves: How do they treat suppliers when cash is tight? Do the books exist, and do they match reality? What happened to the last person who backed them? Then put the agreement in writing — equity split, profit share, reporting cadence, and what happens on the bad day. Friendly deals with vague terms end unfriendly.

Count learning as yield

Your early bets will be tuition; the goal is to make the tuition cheap and the lessons expensive-grade. A small position that teaches you how a sector really works has paid a dividend even at zero. This is how we treat Alttene's own experiments — every build returns either money or a sharper playbook, and compounding needs both.

Play games long enough to win them

Business returns arrive on business time — years, not quarters. The investors who do well in private companies are the ones still there in year five, reinvesting distributions, compounding trust with operators, and sizing every bet so they're never forced to sell the future to survive the present.

Small bets. Long games. Boring on any given day — remarkable on a ten-year chart.
